title: A&P: Cardiovascular & Respiratory
summary: How the heart, the vessels and the lungs actually move oxygen, and how each piece fails. Built from zero to the depth a PA program expects, with every concept tied to something you will see in an emergency department.

lessons.title: The heart: two pumps, four doors
lessons.body:
## Two pumps sharing a wall

The heart is not one pump. It is two pumps bolted together, sharing a wall (the septum) and a single beat. The right side collects blood that has already given up its oxygen and pushes it a short distance into the lungs. The left side takes that freshly loaded blood and pushes it to everything else.

They move the same volume every minute, but at wildly different pressures. The right ventricle squeezes to about `25/5 mmHg`. The left ventricle squeezes to about `120/8 mmHg`. That is why the left ventricular wall is roughly three times thicker, and why the right ventricle fails in a completely different way than the left.

Follow one red cell: body veins, then superior and inferior vena cava, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonic valve, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, body. Note the two exceptions to the rule you were taught in school: the pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying oxygen-poor blood, and the pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygen-rich blood. Artery means away from the heart, not oxygenated.

### Four doors, two sounds

Valves are one-way doors made of thin flaps called leaflets. The two atrioventricular (AV) valves sit between atrium and ventricle: the tricuspid on the right (three leaflets), the mitral on the left (two, which is why it is also called bicuspid). Each is tethered by stringy chordae tendineae to papillary muscles in the ventricle wall, so that when the ventricle squeezes the door slams shut instead of blowing inside out. The two semilunar valves, pulmonic and aortic, are three cups each with no strings; back-pressure alone fills the cups and seals them.

Every normal heart sound is a valve **closing**, never opening. `S1` (the "lub") is mitral and tricuspid slamming at the start of systole. `S2` (the "dub") is aortic and pulmonic snapping shut at the start of diastole. So systole is the space between S1 and S2, and diastole is the longer space from S2 to the next S1.

A murmur is turbulent flow you can hear. Two ways to get it: blood forced through a narrowed valve (stenosis), or blood leaking backward through one that will not seal (regurgitation). Timing names the suspect. A murmur between S1 and S2 is systolic, and the common ones are aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation. A murmur after S2 is diastolic, less common and almost always real disease.

Two extra sounds matter. `S3` is a low thud just after S2 from blood hitting an already full, floppy ventricle, and in an adult it usually means volume overload or heart failure. `S4` comes just before S1, from an atrium pushing against a stiff ventricle, as in long-standing hypertension.

### Three layers and a sac

From the inside out: **endocardium**, the smooth lining continuous with the lining of every vessel, and the surface where infected clumps grow in endocarditis. **Myocardium**, the muscle itself, the layer that dies in a myocardial infarction. **Epicardium**, the thin outer coat.

Wrapping all of it is the pericardium: a tough fibrous outer bag plus a slippery two-leaf serous layer with `15` to `50 mL` of fluid between the leaves. Inflame it (pericarditis) and you get sharp chest pain that eases when the patient leans forward, a scratchy friction rub, and ST elevation in nearly every lead instead of one territory.

Fill it and you get tamponade. Because the fibrous bag cannot stretch quickly, as little as `150` to `200 mL` arriving fast can kill, while a slow effusion can reach `1` to `2 L` before it does harm. The fluid squeezes the low-pressure right side first, so filling (preload) collapses, stroke volume collapses, and pressure follows. Beck's triad is hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart tones. Add tachycardia, a narrow pulse pressure, and pulsus paradoxus (systolic pressure falling more than `10 mmHg` on inspiration). The fix is drainage; a fluid bolus only buys minutes.

> **Key:** Every heart sound is a valve closing. S1 opens systole, S2 closes it, and everything you hear in between or after is named by that timing.

> **On shift:** When you put the diaphragm on a chest, listen at the four valve areas: aortic right second intercostal space, pulmonic left second, tricuspid left lower sternal border, mitral at the apex around the fifth space, midclavicular line.
keyPoints: Right heart is a low-pressure pump to the lungs (about 25/5 mmHg); left heart is high-pressure to the body (about 120/8 mmHg)
Flow: vena cavae, RA, tricuspid, RV, pulmonic, lungs, LA, mitral, LV, aortic, aorta
S1 is the AV valves closing at the start of systole; S2 is the semilunar valves closing at the start of diastole
A murmur is turbulence from a stenotic or regurgitant valve, and its timing names the valve
Tamponade kills through preload: 150 to 200 mL fast gives hypotension, JVD and muffled tones

checks.q: What physically makes the S1 heart sound?
choices: The mitral and tricuspid valves closing as systole begins
The aortic and pulmonic valves opening as blood leaves
The aortic and pulmonic valves closing as diastole begins
Blood striking the wall of a stiff left ventricle
checks.why: Heart sounds are valves closing, never opening. S1 is the AV valves (mitral and tricuspid) slamming shut at the start of systole. Choice 2 describes S2, and choice 3 describes S4.

checks.q: A stabbing victim has a systolic pressure of 78, distended neck veins and heart tones you can barely hear. Which layer or space is the problem?
choices: The endocardium, infected by vegetations
The myocardium, infarcted from a coronary occlusion
The pericardial sac, filling with blood and compressing the heart
The pleural space, filling with air
checks.why: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled tones) is tamponade: blood in the non-stretchy pericardial sac crushes the low-pressure right side and destroys preload. A tension pneumothorax also gives JVD and hypotension, but the tones would not be muffled and breath sounds would be absent on one side.

checks.q: Why does the pulmonary artery carry oxygen-poor blood?
choices: It is a vein that was misnamed historically
Artery means a vessel carrying blood away from the heart, regardless of oxygen content
Oxygen is stripped out as blood passes the pulmonic valve
It carries mixed blood from the shunt between the atria
checks.why: Artery and vein describe direction, not oxygen. The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle heading for the lungs, so it carries deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary veins return loaded blood to the left atrium.

lessons.title: Coronary arteries and the ECG map
lessons.body:
## The heart feeds itself, and only during diastole

Just above the aortic valve, two small holes sit in the wall of the aortic root: the coronary ostia. They are the entrances to the heart's own blood supply. Here is the detail that explains most coronary emergencies: the coronaries fill during **diastole**, when the aortic valve has closed and the muscle is relaxed enough for blood to get into it. Squeezing muscle wrings its own vessels shut.

So anything that shortens diastole, like a heart rate of `160`, or anything that drops diastolic pressure, like shock, starves the heart of its own supply. That is also why the coronary perfusion pressure is roughly aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and why chest compressions that are interrupted let that pressure fall to zero within seconds.

### Three arteries, three territories

**Right coronary artery (RCA)** runs in the groove between right atrium and right ventricle. It supplies the right ventricle, the inferior wall of the left ventricle in most people, and the conduction hardware: the SA node in roughly `60%` of people and the AV node in roughly `85` to `90%`. About `85%` of people are "right dominant," meaning the RCA gives off the posterior descending artery.

**Left anterior descending (LAD)** dives down the front of the heart. It feeds the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the front two-thirds of the septum, and much of the bundle branch system. It supplies more muscle than any other vessel, which is why a proximal LAD occlusion has the nickname widow-maker.

**Left circumflex (LCx)** curls around the left side to the lateral wall, and takes over the posterior wall in the `15%` of people who are left dominant.

### The lead map

A 12-lead ECG is twelve camera angles on the same heart. Group the leads by the wall they look at and the artery names itself.

| Wall | Leads | Usual artery |
|---|---|---|
| Inferior | II, III, aVF | RCA |
| Septal | V1, V2 | LAD |
| Anterior | V3, V4 | LAD |
| Lateral | I, aVL, V5, V6 | LCx |
| Right ventricle | V4R | proximal RCA |
| Posterior | tall R with ST depression in V1 to V3, confirm V7 to V9 | RCA or LCx |

ST elevation in two anatomically contiguous leads is the electrical fingerprint of a full-thickness occlusion in that territory. Reciprocal ST depression in the opposite leads (inferior elevation with depression in I and aVL) makes it more convincing, not less.

### Why an inferior MI arrives slow and soft

Occlude the RCA and you cut the supply to the SA and AV nodes. The result is bradycardia, sinus arrest, and AV blocks, often within minutes. That is the same artery, not a coincidence.

Up to `40%` of inferior MIs also involve the right ventricle. An infarcted right ventricle is a floppy, passive tube that cannot generate pressure; its only way to move blood is to be filled generously. Give that patient nitroglycerin, which works by dumping preload into the venous system, and the pressure falls off a cliff.

So the rule is mechanical, not memorized: ST elevation in II, III and aVF means get a right-sided lead (`V4R`) before nitrates, and if the right ventricle is involved, treat hypotension with fluid rather than vasodilators.

> **Key:** RCA equals inferior wall plus right ventricle plus the nodes. LAD equals anterior wall plus septum. Circumflex equals lateral wall.

> **Trap:** Hypotension in an inferior MI is usually not left ventricular pump failure. It is an empty, stiff right ventricle, and the answer is volume, not a diuretic.
keyPoints: Coronaries fill during diastole, so tachycardia and hypotension both starve the myocardium
RCA: inferior wall, right ventricle, SA node in about 60% and AV node in about 85 to 90%
LAD: anterior wall and anterior septum; LCx: lateral wall
Lead groups: II, III, aVF inferior; V1 to V2 septal; V3 to V4 anterior; I, aVL, V5, V6 lateral
Inferior MI brings bradycardia and blocks, and up to 40% involve the RV, so check V4R before nitroglycerin

checks.q: ST elevation appears in leads II, III and aVF. Which artery is most likely occluded and which wall is infarcting?
choices: LAD, anterior wall
Circumflex, lateral wall
RCA, inferior wall
Left main, entire left ventricle
checks.why: II, III and aVF are the inferior lead group, fed by the RCA in the roughly 85% of people who are right dominant. Anterior would be V3 and V4, lateral would be I, aVL, V5 and V6.

checks.q: Why is nitroglycerin dangerous in a right ventricular infarct?
choices: It causes reflex bradycardia through the AV node
It reduces preload, and the infarcted right ventricle depends entirely on filling
It increases myocardial oxygen demand by raising afterload
It blocks the coronary ostia from filling in diastole
checks.why: Nitrates are venodilators first. They pool blood in the venous system and drop preload. A stunned RV cannot generate its own pressure, so it lives on volume; remove the volume and cardiac output collapses.

lessons.title: The cardiac cycle and the pump math
lessons.body:
## One beat, four phases

Every beat is fill, squeeze, eject, relax. Getting the order right makes the numbers make sense.

1. **Filling (diastole).** AV valves open, blood pours from atria into ventricles. About `70` to `80%` is passive. The atrial kick at the end adds the last `20` to `30%`, which is why losing organized atrial activity in atrial fibrillation can drop output noticeably in a stiff heart.
2. **Isovolumetric contraction.** The ventricle starts to squeeze with all four valves shut. No blood moves, so no volume changes, but pressure climbs fast. This is where most oxygen is consumed.
3. **Ejection (systole).** Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens, and blood leaves.
4. **Isovolumetric relaxation.** Aortic valve shuts (that is S2), all valves closed again, pressure falls until it drops below atrial pressure and the mitral valve opens to start the next fill.

At a rate of `75`, one cycle takes about `0.8 s`: roughly `0.3 s` of systole and `0.5 s` of diastole. Speed the heart up and diastole is what gets cut, which costs filling time and coronary perfusion at the same time.

### The three dials

**Preload** is how stretched the ventricle is just before it squeezes, which really means how much volume is in it at end-diastole. Raised by volume, venous tone and lying flat; lowered by hemorrhage, dehydration, nitrates and anything that blocks venous return.

**Afterload** is the pressure the ventricle must beat to open the aortic valve and eject. Mostly systemic vascular resistance, plus aortic valve disease. Raised by vasoconstriction and hypertension; lowered by vasodilators and by warm, septic vessels.

**Contractility** is the squeeze strength at any given stretch. Raised by sympathetic stimulation, epinephrine, dobutamine and calcium; lowered by ischemia, acidosis, hypoxia and beta blockers.

The **Frank-Starling relationship** ties preload to output: within limits, the more you stretch the muscle before it contracts, the harder it contracts, because the actin and myosin filaments overlap more efficiently. In plain words, a fuller heart squeezes harder. Overstretch it, as in decompensated heart failure, and the curve flattens and falls; now more volume just backs up into the lungs.

### The numbers you will use every shift

**Stroke volume (SV)** is the milliliters ejected per beat, normally `60` to `100 mL`, call it `70 mL`.

**Ejection fraction (EF)** is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally `55` to `70%`. A ventricle holding `120 mL` and ejecting `70 mL` has an EF near `58%`. Note that EF is a fraction, not a flow: a failing heart that has dilated to `250 mL` and ejects `75 mL` has an EF of `30%` but nearly normal stroke volume, which is exactly how patients compensate for a while.

**Cardiac output (CO) = SV x HR.** `70 mL x 70 beats` is about `4.9 L/min`, the familiar "about `5 L/min`" at rest, rising to `20` to `25 L/min` in a trained athlete.

**Mean arterial pressure (MAP) = CO x SVR.** This is the whole hemodynamic universe in four letters: pressure is flow times resistance. Every vasoactive drug you will ever give moves one of those two terms.

At the bedside you estimate MAP from the cuff: `MAP = DBP + 1/3 (SBP - DBP)`. For `120/80`, that is `80 + 1/3(40)`, about `93 mmHg`. The one-third weighting exists because the heart spends about two-thirds of the cycle in diastole, so diastolic pressure counts more.

MAP matters more than systolic because organs are perfused by mean pressure. Below roughly `MAP 65`, the kidney, brain and gut lose their ability to autoregulate flow, and perfusion starts to track pressure directly. That is why `65` is the resuscitation floor in nearly every sepsis and shock protocol.

> **Key:** CO = SV x HR, and MAP = CO x SVR. Every drug and every intervention moves preload, afterload, contractility, rate or resistance. There is nothing else.

> **On the exam:** If a stem gives you a blood pressure and asks about perfusion, compute the MAP before you answer. `90/40` looks survivable and gives a MAP of about `57`.
keyPoints: The cycle is fill, isovolumetric contraction, eject, isovolumetric relaxation; tachycardia steals diastole
Preload is stretch before the squeeze, afterload is the pressure to beat, contractility is squeeze strength at a given stretch
Frank-Starling: a fuller heart squeezes harder, until overstretch flattens the curve
SV 60 to 100 mL, EF 55 to 70%, CO = SV x HR is about 5 L/min at rest
MAP = CO x SVR, estimated as DBP + 1/3 pulse pressure, with 65 mmHg as the perfusion floor

checks.q: A patient's blood pressure is 84/50. What is the approximate MAP?
choices: 50 mmHg
61 mmHg
67 mmHg
84 mmHg
checks.why: MAP = DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) = 50 + 1/3(34) = 50 + 11, about 61 mmHg. That is below the 65 mmHg perfusion floor, so this patient is hypoperfusing even though the systolic looks almost tolerable.

checks.q: A dilated failing heart holds 250 mL at end-diastole and ejects 75 mL. What is true?
choices: EF is 30% and stroke volume is nearly normal
EF is 30% and stroke volume is severely reduced
EF is 70% because stroke volume is normal
EF cannot be calculated without the heart rate
checks.why: EF = 75/250 = 30%, but stroke volume of 75 mL sits inside the normal 60 to 100 mL range. Dilating to preserve stroke volume at a low ejection fraction is exactly how chronic heart failure compensates. Heart rate is needed for cardiac output, not for EF.

checks.q: Which change would raise afterload?
choices: A 1 L normal saline bolus
Nitroglycerin sublingual
A norepinephrine infusion tightening the arterioles
Sepsis with widespread vasodilation
checks.why: Afterload is the resistance the ventricle ejects against, driven mostly by SVR. Norepinephrine constricts arterioles and raises it. Saline raises preload, nitroglycerin lowers preload and afterload, and sepsis lowers SVR.

lessons.title: Conduction, action potentials and the electrolytes that break them
lessons.body:
## A wire that makes its own current

Most cells sit and wait to be told what to do. Cardiac pacemaker cells leak sodium and calcium inward during rest, so their voltage drifts upward on its own until it trips a threshold and fires. That drift is why the heart beats in a jar with no nerves attached.

The pathway, in order: **SA node** in the upper right atrium fires and the impulse spreads across both atria. It funnels into the **AV node** at the floor of the right atrium, which deliberately slows conduction by about `0.1 s`. That pause is the whole reason atria empty into ventricles before the ventricles squeeze, and it is the `PR interval` on the ECG (normal `0.12` to `0.20 s`). From there the **bundle of His** carries the signal into the septum, splits into **right and left bundle branches**, and fans out into **Purkinje fibers** that depolarize the ventricles from the apex upward, so the ventricle wrings out from the bottom like squeezing a tube of toothpaste.

Every piece can pace if the piece above it quits, but slower: SA node `60` to `100`, AV junction `40` to `60`, ventricular or Purkinje escape `20` to `40`. A patient with a heart rate of `35` and no P waves is not simply "bradycardic"; a backup pacemaker has taken over because the primary one failed.

### The action potential, at recognition level

In a working ventricular muscle cell:

- **Phase 0** is the spike: voltage-gated sodium channels fly open, sodium floods in, the cell depolarizes. This is the QRS.
- **Phase 1** is a brief notch as those sodium channels close and a little potassium leaves.
- **Phase 2** is the plateau, unique to cardiac muscle: calcium enters slowly through L-type channels while potassium leaves, and the two nearly cancel. That calcium is what actually triggers contraction, and the plateau's length is why heart muscle cannot be tetanized.
- **Phase 3** is repolarization: calcium channels close, potassium keeps leaving, voltage falls. This is the T wave.
- **Phase 4** is the resting membrane potential, held near `-90 mV` by the sodium-potassium ATPase, or in pacemaker cells the slow upward drift described above.

Three ions, three clinical stories.

**Potassium** sets the resting potential and dominates repolarization. High potassium (hyperkalemia) makes repolarization fast and steep: the earliest ECG sign is **tall, peaked, narrow T waves**, usually above `5.5 mEq/L`. Keep climbing and the P wave flattens and disappears, the PR stretches, the QRS widens, and finally the tracing turns into a sine wave and arrests. Low potassium does the opposite, flattening the T wave and producing a U wave, and it predisposes to torsades.

**Calcium** drives phase 2 and therefore contraction. Calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem and verapamil slow AV nodal conduction and reduce contractility, which is exactly why they control rate in atrial fibrillation and exactly why they are dangerous in a failing ventricle. Low serum calcium lengthens the `QT`; high calcium shortens it.

**Sodium** drives phase 0. Anything that blocks the fast sodium channel slows the upstroke and widens the QRS. This is the mechanism behind tricyclic antidepressant overdose: a QRS wider than `100 ms` predicts seizures, wider than `160 ms` predicts ventricular arrhythmia, and sodium bicarbonate works by raising serum sodium and pH to push sodium back through the channel.

> **Key:** Potassium sets the resting voltage and the T wave, calcium runs the plateau and contraction, sodium runs the upstroke and the QRS width.

> **On shift:** Peaked T waves on a dialysis patient who missed a session is hyperkalemia until proven otherwise. Calcium gluconate stabilizes the membrane in minutes without lowering the potassium at all, and that distinction is a favorite exam question.
keyPoints: Order: SA node, AV node with its 0.1 s delay, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
Intrinsic rates: SA 60 to 100, AV junction 40 to 60, ventricular escape 20 to 40
Phase 0 sodium in (QRS), phase 2 calcium plateau (contraction), phase 3 potassium out (T wave), phase 4 rest at about -90 mV
Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves first, then flat P, wide QRS, sine wave
Sodium channel blockade (tricyclics) widens the QRS; bicarbonate is the antidote mechanism

checks.q: What is the purpose of the AV node's 0.1 second delay?
choices: To let the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before ventricular contraction
To prevent the SA node from firing too fast
To allow calcium to enter during the plateau phase
To create the T wave on the ECG
checks.why: The delay is the mechanical reason atrial kick works: it holds the signal long enough for the atria to finish loading the ventricles. On the ECG it is most of the PR interval, normally 0.12 to 0.20 s.

checks.q: A missed-dialysis patient has tall, narrow, peaked T waves. Which ion is the problem and what happens next if it is untreated?
choices: Low calcium, progressing to a prolonged QT
High potassium, progressing to a wide QRS and sine wave
Low potassium, progressing to U waves
High sodium, progressing to a narrow QRS
checks.why: Peaked T waves are the first ECG sign of hyperkalemia, typically above 5.5 mEq/L. The progression is loss of P waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening, then a sine wave and arrest. Hypokalemia produces flat T waves and U waves instead.

checks.q: An overdose patient has a QRS of 150 ms after taking amitriptyline. What is the mechanism?
choices: Calcium channel blockade slowing the AV node
Potassium efflux blockade lengthening repolarization only
Fast sodium channel blockade slowing phase 0 depolarization
Beta blockade reducing contractility
checks.why: Tricyclics block the fast sodium channel that drives phase 0, so the ventricular upstroke is slow and the QRS widens. Above 100 ms predicts seizures and above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia, which is why sodium bicarbonate is given.

lessons.title: Vessels, capillary exchange and venous return
lessons.body:
## Four different jobs, four different walls

Every vessel has the same three coats: an inner endothelium (tunica intima), a middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic tissue (tunica media), and an outer connective sheath (tunica externa). The proportions decide the job.

**Elastic arteries** like the aorta are mostly elastic tissue. They balloon out during systole and recoil during diastole, which is what keeps blood flowing forward while the heart is refilling. Lose that elasticity with age and systolic pressure rises, diastolic falls, and the pulse pressure widens.

**Arterioles** are almost all smooth muscle, and they are the story. Because resistance goes up with the fourth power of the radius, a small change in arteriolar diameter changes flow enormously. Halve the radius and resistance rises sixteenfold. Arterioles are therefore the **resistance vessels**, the SVR in `MAP = CO x SVR`, and the target of nearly every vasopressor and antihypertensive.

**Capillaries** are one endothelial cell thick, about `5` to `10 micrometers` across, so red cells pass single file. That is the only place in the entire circulation where anything is exchanged. Everything else is plumbing.

**Veins** are thin-walled, floppy, and equipped with one-way valves. They are **capacitance vessels**: at rest they hold about `60` to `70%` of the entire blood volume, which makes the venous system the body's reservoir.

### Starling forces, in plain words

At the capillary, two forces push fluid out and two pull it back.

- **Hydrostatic pressure** inside the capillary is the blood pressure pushing water out through the leaky wall. It runs about `35 mmHg` at the arterial end and falls to about `15 mmHg` at the venous end.
- **Oncotic pressure** is the pull of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, holding water in. It is roughly constant at about `25 mmHg`.

So at the arterial end, push beats pull and fluid filters out into the tissue. At the venous end, pull beats push and most of it comes back. The small remainder, roughly `2` to `4 L` a day, is picked up by lymphatics.

Edema is that balance broken, and there are only four ways to break it:

1. Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, as in heart failure or a venous clot. Backed-up pressure pushes more fluid out.
2. Lowered plasma oncotic pressure, as in liver failure, nephrotic syndrome or malnutrition. Not enough albumin to pull water back.
3. Increased capillary permeability, as in sepsis, burns or anaphylaxis. The wall itself starts leaking protein, so oncotic pressure equalizes across the wall and water follows.
4. Blocked lymphatic drainage, as after axillary node dissection.

That list is the entire differential for a swollen limb, and it tells you why albumin does not fix septic edema (the wall is leaking) but volume does raise pressure.

### Getting blood back uphill

Venous pressure is only about `8` to `10 mmHg` at the venules and near `0` at the right atrium. That is not enough to lift blood from the feet, so four mechanisms help: the **skeletal muscle pump** (calf contractions squeeze veins, one-way valves keep the flow headed up), the **respiratory pump** (inhaling drops intrathoracic pressure and sucks blood toward the chest), **venoconstriction** from sympathetic tone, and the residual push from the heart itself.

This matters clinically. Standing still for an hour lets blood pool, preload falls, and people faint. Valve failure gives varicose veins and chronic venous stasis. Immobility gives stagnation, which is one leg of Virchow's triad for clot formation.

> **Key:** Arterioles control resistance and therefore pressure. Veins hold volume. Capillaries are the only place exchange happens.

> **Trap:** "Third spacing" in sepsis is not a fluid overload problem, it is a leaky-wall problem. The intravascular space can be empty while the tissues are waterlogged.
keyPoints: Arterioles are the resistance vessels; resistance varies with the fourth power of radius
Veins are capacitance vessels holding 60 to 70% of blood volume
Capillary hydrostatic pressure is about 35 mmHg arterial and 15 mmHg venous; oncotic pull is about 25 mmHg
Four causes of edema: high hydrostatic, low oncotic, leaky wall, blocked lymphatics
Venous return depends on the muscle pump, the respiratory pump and venous tone, not on heart pressure alone

checks.q: A patient with cirrhosis has an albumin of 1.9 g/dL and swollen legs. Which Starling force changed?
choices: Capillary hydrostatic pressure rose
Plasma oncotic pressure fell, so less fluid is pulled back in
Lymphatic drainage was surgically removed
Interstitial oncotic pressure fell
checks.why: Albumin generates the roughly 25 mmHg oncotic pull that returns fluid at the venous end of the capillary. A failing liver makes less of it, so fluid stays in the tissue. Hydrostatic pressure rises in heart failure or venous obstruction, not in low-albumin states.

checks.q: Why does a small change in arteriolar diameter change blood pressure so much?
choices: Arterioles contain most of the blood volume
Arterioles are the only site of gas exchange
Resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius
Arterioles have no smooth muscle, so they collapse easily
checks.why: Resistance is inversely proportional to radius to the fourth power, so halving the radius raises resistance about sixteenfold. Veins hold the volume; capillaries do the exchange; arterioles are thick with smooth muscle, which is how they change radius at all.

lessons.title: Blood pressure control: reflexes, RAAS and the peptides
lessons.body:
## Two systems, two time scales

Blood pressure is defended by a fast neural system that works in seconds and a slow hormonal system that works in minutes to days. Knowing which one a drug touches is most of cardiovascular pharmacology.

### Seconds: the baroreflex

Stretch receptors (baroreceptors) sit in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch. They fire continuously, and their firing rate reports the pressure they feel. The signal travels to the medulla by cranial nerve IX from the carotid and cranial nerve X from the aorta.

When pressure falls, the receptors stretch less and fire less. The medulla reads that reduced traffic as a loss of pressure and answers by withdrawing parasympathetic tone and increasing sympathetic outflow. The result is more heart rate (beta-1), more contractility (beta-1), arteriolar constriction (alpha-1) raising SVR, and venoconstriction (alpha-1) squeezing the venous reservoir back toward the heart to restore preload. All four terms in `MAP = CO x SVR` move the same direction.

This is why the first vital sign to change in early hemorrhage is heart rate, not pressure. The reflex holds the pressure normal while the tank empties. Narrowing pulse pressure, cool skin and delayed capillary refill are the reflex working, and blood pressure falls only when it has run out of slack, usually after about `30%` of blood volume is gone. A patient on a beta blocker cannot mount the tachycardia, which is why they crash without warning.

### Minutes to days: RAAS

The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is one chain with four clinically important links.

1. The kidney's **juxtaglomerular cells** sense low renal perfusion, low sodium delivery, or sympathetic stimulation, and release **renin**.
2. Renin cleaves **angiotensinogen** (made by the liver) into **angiotensin I**, which does almost nothing.
3. **Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)**, mostly in the lung endothelium, converts angiotensin I into **angiotensin II**.
4. Angiotensin II is the effector: it is a potent arteriolar vasoconstrictor, it stimulates thirst, it triggers ADH release, and it tells the adrenal cortex to release **aldosterone**, which makes the distal nephron reabsorb sodium and water while dumping potassium.

So RAAS raises pressure twice over: resistance up, and volume up.

Drugs land on specific links. **ACE inhibitors** (lisinopril, enalapril) block step 3. Because ACE also degrades bradykinin, blocking it lets bradykinin accumulate, which is the mechanism of the dry cough in `5` to `20%` of patients and of ACE inhibitor angioedema. **ARBs** (losartan, valsartan) block the angiotensin II receptor itself, so they skip the bradykinin problem. **Spironolactone** blocks aldosterone, which is why it spares potassium. **Beta blockers** also reduce renin release from the kidney.

### The counter-regulators

**Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin)** comes from the posterior pituitary in response to high plasma osmolality or a big volume loss. It makes the collecting duct reabsorb free water, and at high doses it constricts vessels, which is why vasopressin appears as a second-line pressor in septic shock.

**Natriuretic peptides** are the brake. When atrial or ventricular walls are stretched by volume, cardiac muscle releases **ANP** (atria) and **BNP** (ventricles). They do the opposite of RAAS: they dump sodium and water at the kidney, dilate vessels, and suppress renin and aldosterone.

That is why `BNP` is a useful lab. A dyspneic patient whose ventricles are stretched by fluid overload has a high BNP; one whose shortness of breath is from COPD usually does not. A `BNP` under about `100 pg/mL` argues strongly against acute heart failure, while values over `400 to 500 pg/mL` support it. Kidney failure and age raise it independently, so it is one input, not a verdict.

> **Key:** Baroreflex handles seconds through the sympathetic nervous system. RAAS handles minutes to days through resistance and volume. Natriuretic peptides push the other way.

> **On the exam:** If asked where an ACE inhibitor acts, the answer is the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which happens mostly in the pulmonary endothelium.
keyPoints: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire less when pressure falls, triggering sympathetic outflow within seconds
Early hemorrhage shows tachycardia and narrow pulse pressure; pressure falls only after roughly 30% volume loss
RAAS chain: renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, aldosterone; it raises both resistance and volume
ACE inhibitors block step 3 and cause cough and angioedema through bradykinin; ARBs block the receptor instead
BNP is released by stretched ventricles; under 100 pg/mL argues against acute heart failure

checks.q: A trauma patient has lost about 1 L of blood. Heart rate is 118, blood pressure 118/92. Why is the pressure still normal?
choices: The bleeding has stopped on its own
The baroreflex has raised rate, contractility and SVR to defend the pressure
RAAS has already replaced the lost volume
Blood pressure only falls with arterial bleeding
checks.why: The baroreflex compensates within seconds, and the narrow pulse pressure (26) is the tell: the diastolic is being held up by arteriolar constriction. Pressure typically holds until roughly 30% of volume is lost. RAAS cannot replace a liter in minutes.

checks.q: Where does lisinopril act?
choices: It blocks conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
It blocks the angiotensin II receptor
It blocks aldosterone at the distal tubule
It blocks renin release from juxtaglomerular cells
checks.why: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin converting enzyme, largely in pulmonary endothelium. Receptor blockade is an ARB, aldosterone blockade is spironolactone, and direct renin inhibition is aliskiren.

checks.q: Why does BNP rise in acute heart failure?
choices: The kidneys release it in response to low perfusion
The liver produces it when congested
Stretched ventricular muscle releases it as a counter-regulatory hormone
It is released by the adrenal cortex alongside aldosterone
checks.why: BNP comes from ventricular myocardium stretched by volume, and it opposes RAAS by promoting sodium and water loss and vasodilation. ANP is the atrial version. Renin is the kidney hormone; aldosterone is adrenal.

lessons.title: Shock: five failures of one equation
lessons.body:
## Shock is not low blood pressure

Shock is inadequate delivery of oxygen to tissue. Blood pressure is a late, crude proxy for it. A patient can be in shock with a normal pressure (compensated) and can have a low pressure without being in shock (a healthy young athlete asleep).

Delivery has three requirements: enough volume to pump, a pump that works, and a circuit with appropriate resistance. `MAP = CO x SVR` and `CO = SV x HR`. Every shock state is one of those terms failing, and each failure leaves a distinct hemodynamic fingerprint.

### The five fingerprints

| Type | Preload | Contractility | CO | SVR | Skin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypovolemic | low | normal | low | high | cool, pale |
| Cardiogenic | high | low | low | high | cool, mottled |
| Distributive (septic, anaphylactic) | low | normal or high | high early, low late | low | warm, flushed early |
| Neurogenic | low | low or normal | low | low | warm, dry, pink |
| Obstructive | low reaching the LV | normal | low | high | cool |

Read the table as a decision tool. Cool and clamped means the body is compensating by constricting, so the problem is volume or pump. Warm and dilated means resistance itself has failed.

**Hypovolemic** is lost volume: hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea, burns, DKA. Preload falls, the reflex raises rate and SVR, pulse pressure narrows, and neck veins are flat.

**Cardiogenic** is a pump that cannot eject, most often a large anterior MI. Preload is high and backs up, so you see distended neck veins and wet lungs with a low pressure. That combination, hypotension plus JVD plus crackles, is the fingerprint.

**Distributive** is lost resistance. Septic shock: infection triggers inflammatory mediators that dilate arterioles and make capillaries leak, so SVR falls and volume leaves the vessels. Anaphylaxis: mast cell histamine does the same thing in minutes, plus bronchospasm and airway swelling. Neurogenic shock: a cord injury above about `T6` cuts sympathetic outflow, so vessels dilate and the heart cannot even mount a compensatory tachycardia, giving the classic hypotension **with** bradycardia and warm dry skin.

**Obstructive** is a mechanical block in the circuit despite a normal pump and normal volume. Tension pneumothorax kinks venous return, tamponade compresses filling, and a massive pulmonary embolism blocks the outlet so the right ventricle fails acutely.

### The stages

**Compensated.** The reflexes are winning. Normal pressure, tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, anxiety or restlessness, cool extremities, delayed capillary refill over `2 s`, and falling urine output under `0.5 mL/kg/h`. This is where shock is cheap to fix and easy to miss.

**Decompensated.** The reflexes lose. Hypotension appears, mentation dulls, skin mottles, lactate climbs, and acidosis begins to blunt the response to catecholamines.

**Irreversible.** Cell death, capillary sludging and multi-organ failure continue even after pressure is restored. There is no sharp line, which is the argument for treating stage one aggressively.

### Lactate, the perfusion meter

When a cell cannot get oxygen, it runs pyruvate to lactate instead of into the mitochondria. Lactate is therefore a direct readout of anaerobic metabolism. Normal is under `2 mmol/L`; over `4 mmol/L` marks severe tissue hypoperfusion and, with suspected infection, defines septic shock together with pressors. Serial lactates matter more than a single value: a level that clears by `10` to `20%` after resuscitation says you are winning.

### Why norepinephrine

Septic shock is primarily an SVR problem with a leaky, underfilled circuit. So the first move is volume, typically `30 mL/kg` of balanced crystalloid, and if MAP stays under `65 mmHg`, the first-line vasopressor is **norepinephrine**. It is a strong alpha-1 agonist that restores SVR with modest beta-1 support, so it raises pressure without the heavy tachycardia and arrhythmia burden of dopamine or pure epinephrine. Vasopressin is added second to spare the norepinephrine dose.

> **Key:** Name the failing term first. Volume, pump, or pipes. The physical exam finding that separates them is the skin plus the neck veins.

> **Trap:** Hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin after a diving injury is neurogenic shock, not hemorrhage, but trauma patients can have both, so bleeding is still ruled out first.
keyPoints: Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery, not a blood pressure number; compensated shock has a normal pressure
Cool and clamped means low volume or a failing pump; warm and dilated means low SVR
Cardiogenic gives hypotension with JVD and crackles; hypovolemic gives hypotension with flat neck veins
Neurogenic shock is the one hypotension that comes with bradycardia and warm dry skin
Lactate over 4 mmol/L marks severe hypoperfusion; norepinephrine is first-line in septic shock after 30 mL/kg fluid

checks.q: A febrile 70-year-old has BP 82/38, HR 122, warm flushed skin, flat neck veins and a lactate of 5.1 mmol/L. Which term of MAP = CO x SVR has failed?
choices: Contractility, giving cardiogenic shock
SVR, giving distributive shock
Preload from mechanical obstruction
Heart rate, giving bradycardic shock
checks.why: Warm skin with a very wide pulse pressure (44 on a low mean) and flat neck veins says the vessels are dilated and the circuit is underfilled, which is distributive. Cardiogenic would be cool and mottled with distended neck veins; obstructive would be cool with high SVR.

checks.q: Which finding best separates cardiogenic from hypovolemic shock at the bedside?
choices: Heart rate
Skin temperature
Jugular venous distension and lung crackles
Capillary refill time
checks.why: Both are cool and tachycardic with delayed refill because both trigger the same sympathetic response. The difference is preload: cardiogenic backs blood up behind a failing pump so the neck veins fill and the lungs get wet, while hypovolemia empties them.

checks.q: Why is norepinephrine first-line in septic shock?
choices: It is a pure beta-1 agonist that raises cardiac output
It restores SVR through alpha-1 with less tachyarrhythmia than dopamine
It seals leaking capillaries directly
It lowers lactate by blocking anaerobic metabolism
checks.why: The core defect in septic shock is a collapsed SVR, so an alpha-1 dominant agent is the physiologic match. Norepinephrine produces fewer arrhythmias than dopamine at equivalent pressure support. Nothing seals capillaries directly, and lactate falls only when perfusion improves.

lessons.title: Respiratory anatomy and the mechanics of breathing
lessons.body:
## Two zones, one purpose

Air travels nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, then branches about 23 times: main bronchi, lobar bronchi, segmental bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli. There are roughly `300` to `500 million` alveoli, giving a gas exchange surface of about `70 square meters`.

Split that tree into two zones. The **conducting zone** runs from the nose to the terminal bronchioles: it warms, humidifies and filters air, but has no alveoli, so nothing is exchanged there. That volume is **anatomic dead space**, roughly `2 mL/kg`, about `150 mL` in an average adult. The **respiratory zone** begins at the respiratory bronchioles, where alveoli appear in the wall, and it is the only part that does the job.

That `150 mL` is the most useful number in respiratory physiology. A tidal volume of `500 mL` moves only `350 mL` of fresh gas to the alveoli. Rapid shallow breathing, say `150 mL` at a rate of `40`, moves `6 L/min` of air and essentially zero fresh gas to the alveoli.

### Lobes, fissures and where to listen

The right lung has three lobes and two fissures; the left has two lobes and one, plus a lingula, because the heart occupies the space. The oblique fissure runs on both sides from roughly the T3 spinous process down and forward to the sixth rib. The right horizontal fissure runs at about the fourth rib.

That geometry decides where you hear things. On the anterior chest above the fourth rib you are listening to upper lobes. On the posterior chest below the scapular spine you are mostly hearing lower lobes. The right middle lobe is heard anteriorly and laterally at the right fourth to sixth spaces and nowhere on the back. A patient with a right middle lobe pneumonia can have a completely clear posterior exam.

Between the lungs is the **mediastinum**, holding heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus and thymus. The **diaphragm** is the main muscle of breathing, driven by the phrenic nerve from roots `C3, C4 and C5`, which is why a cord injury above C3 stops breathing and the mnemonic "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive" survives.

### Pressure moves air

Each lung sits in a sealed bag of two membranes: the visceral pleura stuck to the lung and the parietal pleura lining the chest wall, with a few milliliters of fluid between. That fluid couples them like two wet glass slides, so when the chest wall expands, the lung must follow.

The pleural space sits at a negative pressure, about `-5 cm H2O` at rest and about `-8` at full inspiration, because the elastic lung always wants to collapse inward while the chest wall wants to spring outward. Break the seal with air (pneumothorax) and the tether is gone; the lung recoils inward and collapses.

Inspiration is active: the diaphragm flattens and drops, external intercostals lift the ribs, thoracic volume rises, alveolar pressure falls to about `-1 cm H2O` below atmospheric, and air flows in. Normal expiration is passive elastic recoil. Forced expiration adds the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals.

Two properties fight you. **Compliance** is how easily the lung stretches; it falls in pulmonary fibrosis, ARDS and pulmonary edema, and rises abnormally in emphysema where destroyed elastic tissue gives a floppy lung that fills easily and will not empty. **Resistance** is how hard air is to push through the tubes; it rises in asthma, bronchospasm and any obstruction. Either one raises the **work of breathing**, which normally consumes about `2` to `5%` of resting oxygen use and can reach `30%` or more in respiratory distress. When those muscles finally fail, you get the ominous sequence of a slowing respiratory rate with a rising CO2.

### The volumes

| Measure | Typical adult | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Tidal volume (VT) | `500 mL` (`6` to `8 mL/kg`) | one normal breath |
| Inspiratory reserve (IRV) | `3000 mL` | extra you can pull in |
| Expiratory reserve (ERV) | `1100 mL` | extra you can push out |
| Residual volume (RV) | `1200 mL` | never leaves the lung |
| Vital capacity (VC) | `4600 mL` | VT + IRV + ERV |
| Functional residual capacity (FRC) | `2300 mL` | ERV + RV, what is left after a normal breath out |
| Total lung capacity (TLC) | `5800 mL` | everything |

FRC is the body's oxygen reservoir between breaths. Anything that shrinks it (obesity, late pregnancy, ascites, lying flat) means less stored oxygen, so a preoxygenated patient desaturates in seconds rather than minutes once breathing stops.

Finally, **minute ventilation = VT x RR**, about `6 L/min`, while **alveolar ventilation = (VT - dead space) x RR**, about `4.2 L/min`. Only the second one clears CO2.

> **Key:** Anatomic dead space is about `150 mL`, so tidal volume and rate are not interchangeable. Deeper is more efficient than faster.

> **On shift:** A pregnant or obese patient at the end of the bed is the one you preoxygenate longest and position upright, because the FRC that would have bought you time is not there.
keyPoints: Conducting zone (nose to terminal bronchioles) is anatomic dead space, about 2 mL/kg or 150 mL
Minute ventilation is VT x RR, but only alveolar ventilation, (VT - 150) x RR, clears CO2
Pleural pressure is about -5 cm H2O at rest; breaking the seal lets the elastic lung collapse
Compliance falls in fibrosis, ARDS and edema; resistance rises in asthma and obstruction
FRC is about 2300 mL of stored oxygen, and it shrinks in obesity and pregnancy, so those patients desaturate fast

checks.q: A patient breathes 150 mL tidal volumes at a rate of 40. Minute ventilation is 6 L/min. What is alveolar ventilation?
choices: About 6 L/min, which is normal
About 4.2 L/min, which is normal
About 0 L/min, because tidal volume barely exceeds dead space
About 2 L/min, which is adequate
checks.why: Alveolar ventilation is (VT - dead space) x RR = (150 - 150) x 40 = 0. All that effort is moving the same 150 mL of dead-space gas back and forth. The minute ventilation looks normal, which is exactly why the number deceives.

checks.q: Why does an obese patient desaturate within seconds of apnea despite good preoxygenation?
choices: Reduced functional residual capacity means a smaller stored oxygen reservoir
Reduced residual volume means the lungs fully empty
Increased anatomic dead space dilutes the oxygen
Increased compliance traps oxygen in the alveoli
checks.why: Abdominal mass pushes the diaphragm up and squeezes out expiratory reserve volume, shrinking FRC. FRC is the oxygen the lung holds between breaths, so a smaller FRC means a shorter safe apnea time. Dead space and compliance are not the primary problem here.

checks.q: Which nerve roots supply the diaphragm?
choices: T1 through T4
C1 and C2
C3, C4 and C5
C7 and C8
checks.why: The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5. A spinal cord injury above that level knocks out spontaneous breathing entirely; injuries below it spare the diaphragm but may cost the intercostals and abdominal muscles.
